claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 mild steel has a naturally formed native oxide layer.
The native oxide layer is sub-micrometer in thickness and passive.
At room temperature, the native oxide layer acts as a barrier that suppresses corrosion in chloride-rich harsh environments.
The native oxide film limits chloride ingress into Q235 steel.
Limiting chloride ingress slows the corrosion of Q235 steel.
Exposure at approximately 80°C generates thermal stress that compromises the integrity of the native oxide film.
Elevated-temperature exposure causes microcracking of the native oxide film.
Elevated-temperature exposure increases the porosity of the native oxide film.
Microcracking and increased porosity permit greater ingress of corrosive species.
Greater ingress of corrosive species increases corrosion degradation.
Oxide-free polished Q235 steel has relatively high corrosion because the metal is directly exposed to the chloride-rich environment.
At room temperature, native-oxide-bearing samples will have less weight loss than oxide-free polished samples.
At room temperature, native-oxide-bearing samples will have fewer pitting sites than oxide-free polished samples.
At 80°C, initially native-oxide-bearing samples will show greater weight loss and pit density than their room-temperature counterparts.
At 80°C, initially native-oxide-bearing samples will show degraded oxide morphology relative to their room-temperature counterparts.
At 80°C, oxide-compromised samples will corrode more rapidly than oxide-free polished samples.
A factorial comparison of native-oxide and polished surfaces at 25°C and 80°C for 72 hours can isolate the effects of temperature and initial surface condition.
SEM and XPS can assess changes in oxide-film morphology and composition.
Weight loss, pit density, pit depth, and electrochemical polarization can measure corrosion degradation and kinetics.
The proposed behavior may not apply to coated steels, substantially different alloys, or environments with extreme pH or oxide-altering constituents.

contradictions.description: The mechanism frames oxide removal and direct metal exposure as producing relatively high corrosion, whereas the predicted outcome says the thermally compromised oxide-bearing samples will corrode significantly more than the oxide-free polished samples. The hypothesis does not provide an additional mechanism, such as galvanic localization or chloride trapping, that would explain why a degraded residual film is worse than complete film removal.

The polished oxide-free specimen is called the 'untreated reference,' although mechanical polishing is itself a surface treatment and the as-received native-oxide specimen is the actual untreated material state.
